questions.q: When you perform a point-in-time restore in Azure SQL Database, what actually happens to the original database?
options: Nothing — the restore creates a new database alongside the original, which is never overwritten
The original database is overwritten with the restored data
The original database is deleted and replaced by the restored copy
The original database is paused until the restore completes
questions.explain: Restoring always creates a new database. The typical workflow is to verify the restored copy, then either swap connection strings or copy data back into the original.

questions.q: What is the default length of the point-in-time restore retention window, and how far can it be configured for short-term retention?
options: Defaults to 7 days, configurable up to 35 days
Defaults to 1 day, configurable up to 7 days
Defaults to 30 days, configurable up to 1 year
There is no default — it must always be set manually before first use
questions.explain: The short-term (non-LTR) retention window defaults to 7 days and can be configured up to 35 days depending on tier and settings.

questions.q: If someone deletes an entire Azure SQL Database, where do you go to restore it?
options: The server's "Deleted databases" list — restoring happens at the server level, since the database itself no longer exists
The deleted database's own Overview page, which remains accessible after deletion
You cannot restore a deleted database under any circumstances
The Azure subscription's billing page
questions.explain: Since there's no database left to right-click, Azure retains the deleted database's backup history at the server level, in its Deleted Databases list.

questions.q: Can you restore an Azure SQL Database to a point in time before the earliest backup available in the retention window?
options: No — the timeline picker only allows selecting valid timestamps within the available backup history
Yes, restores can go back indefinitely regardless of retention settings
Yes, but only for databases using long-term retention
Yes, as long as the database uses geo-redundant storage
questions.explain: You're bounded by what backups actually exist. The retention window sets the outer limit of what timestamps are selectable.

questions.q: What underlying mechanism does point-in-time restore rely on to reconstruct a database at an exact moment?
options: The same full-plus-differential-plus-log backup chain logic from earlier in this chapter, applied automatically by Azure
A single full backup taken at the exact moment requested
A manual snapshot the DBA must trigger in advance
Real-time replication to a secondary region
questions.explain: Azure's automated backups (full, differential, log) form the same kind of restore chain covered earlier — point-in-time restore just applies that chain automatically instead of by hand.
